{{short description|American physicist}}
'''Lewis Salter''' (1926–1989) was an American [[theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]], [[physics]] [[physics education|professor]], and researcher. He served as the dean of [[Knox College (Illinois)|Knox College]] for 11 years and was the twelfth president of [[Wabash College]].

==Biography==
Salter was born in [[Norman, Oklahoma|Norman]], [[Oklahoma]]. He spent three years in the [[United States Army]] during [[World War II]], then received his undergraduate education at the [[University of Oklahoma]], where he was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref>{{cite journal|title =Lewis Salter New President of Wabash|journal =Newsletter of the American Scientific Affiliation - Canadian Scientific & Christian Affiliation|volume =20|issue =2|date =April–May 1978|url =http://www.asa3.org/asa/topics/NewsLetter70s/APRMAY78.html|accessdate =2008-01-18|archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20060422102412/http://www.asa3.org/ASA/topics/NewsLetter70s/APRMAY78.html|archive-date =2006-04-22|url-status =dead}}</ref>  He was selected as a [[Rhodes Scholar]], and spent 1949 to 1953 at the [[University of Oxford]], where he received his master's degree and [[Ph.D.|doctorate]] in theoretical physics.<ref name="history"/>

After leaving Oxford, Salter joined the faculty of Wabash College in 1953. He took leave from Wabash from 1958 to 1960 to help establish a research program in theoretical physics at the [[Bandung Institute of Technology]] in [[Indonesia]]. He left Wabash in 1967 to become dean of [[Knox College (Illinois)|Knox College]] He continued his international activities, working for the [[World Bank]] Survey team in [[Indonesia]] and consulting on science education there in 1972, and consulting on science education for the [[United States Agency for International Development]]. Salter was also a physics consultant to the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] and the Canadian National Research Council.
  
Salter returned to Wabash College as its president in 1978. The issue of Wabash remaining an all-male college was addressed multiple times while Salter was president.<ref>{{cite news |title = Campus Life: Wabash; A New President, An Old Debate: Admit Women?|work =[[The New York Times]]|date =1989-12-17 |url =https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/17/style/campus-life-wabash-a-new-president-an-old-debate-admit-women.html|access-date =2008-01-18}}</ref>

After he was diagnosed with terminal cancer, he resigned the presidency of the college and returned to teaching physics in August 1989, but he died before the fall term ended.<ref name="history">{{cite web|last =McAlister|first =Patrick|title =Wabash College's Presidents|work =The Bachelor|publisher =[[Wabash College]]|date =2007-01-25|url =http://bachelor.wabash.edu/issues/2007s/inaugfull1.pdf|accessdate =2008-01-18|archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20070221190101/http://bachelor.wabash.edu/issues/2007s/inaugfull1.pdf|archive-date =2007-02-21|url-status =dead}}</ref> He continued to work on research problems until his death, and had a paper published posthumously in the ''[[American Journal of Physics]]''.
